title: The Forgotten Racial History of Alligator Alcatraz
author: Mark V. Barrow, Jr.
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Florida-
Everglades_National_Park-3-680x510.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/13/the-
forgotten-racial-history-of-alligator-alcatraz/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Florida-
Everglades_National_Park-3-680x510.jpg)

American alligator lurking in the Everglades. Photo: Marine 69-71. Wikimedia.
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0)

The migrant detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz is
[closed](https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/eenews/2026/07/20/desantis-
admin-offers-court-proof-that-alligator-alcatraz-is-really-closed-
ee-01004884), but much about it remains unresolved. There are [lawsuits over
detainees’ treatment](https://www.wflx.com/2026/07/20/federal-judge-weighs-
floridas-assurances-that-alligator-alcatraz-wont-reopen/), environmental
claims over [damage to protected
wetlands](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/18/shuttered-alligator-
alcatraz-leaves-complicated-legacy-in-florida-01001031) and uncertainty about
the [future of the airstrip](https://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/floridas-
alligator-alcatraz-immigration-detention-center-has-closed-governor-
says/3833521/) it was built on.

One aspect of the South Florida facility has drawn far less attention, though:
the name itself, and the long history of associating alligators with racist
ideas about people of color.

I’m a [historian of wildlife](https://experts.vt.edu/2288-mark-barrow), the
environment and American culture who has studied the cultural and
environmental history of the American alligator. My [research
shows](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo268426675.html)
that the species has carried a variety of meanings in the United States,
ranging from a prized source of leather for luxury fashion to an emblem of
Florida identity. Less well known is the reptile’s role in the nation’s
history of racial stereotyping. For generations, alligators featured
prominently in imagery intended to demean Black Americans.

Whatever the intentions of those who named and promoted the facility,
Alligator Alcatraz echoed a long tradition of using alligators in ways that
have reinforced racist imagery and dehumanizing stereotypes.

**Constructing Alligator Alcatraz**

Located on a remote landing strip surrounded by Big Cypress National Preserve,
about 6 miles north of Everglades National Park, Alligator Alcatraz sparked
controversy from the beginning. Critics argued that the detention center
housed immigrants in [unsafe and inhumane
conditions](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2025/12/estados-unidos-
nuevas-investigaciones-revelan-violaciones-de-derechos-humanos-en-los-centros-
de-detencion-de-alligator-alcatraz-y-krome-en-florida/), [limited
access](https://www.findlaw.com/legalblogs/practice-of-law/lawyers-battle-
access-barriers-at-alligator-alcatraz/) for lawyers and family members, and
[imperiled sensitive, federally protected
wetlands](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/26/alligator-alcatraz-
environmental-immigrant-inquiry).
[Seminole](https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/local/state/2025/07/02/seminole-
tribe-calls-alligator-alcatraz-threat-to-sacred-lands-florida/84450024007/)
and [Miccosukee](https://prismreports.org/2025/08/05/alligator-alcatraz-
miccosukee-tribe/) people denounced it as a threat to their sacred homelands.
Some detractors even characterized it as a [concentration
camp](https://www.ms.now/opinion/msnbc-opinion/immigration-alligator-alcatraz-
concentration-camp-rcna216874).

In a [lengthy exposé](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/06/alligator-
alcatraz-desantis-florida-immigration/687415/) for The Atlantic, journalist
Eric Schlosser decried the facility as “a uniquely cruel publicity stunt with
an absurdly high price tag.” Based on figures from court filings and Florida’s
grant application to the Federal Emergency Management Agency, Schlosser
estimated that it cost about US$500,000 a year to hold a single immigrant at
Alligator Alcatraz. By contrast, Florida spends only $30,000 a year to confine
someone in a state prison.

The contentious center was the brainchild of [Florida Attorney General James
Uthmeier](https://abcnews.com/US/florida-attorney-general-proposes-alligator-
alcatraz-migrant-detention/story?id=123149898), who [pitched the idea to
federal officials](https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/5359682-florida-
attorney-general-undocumented-migrants-facility/) in June 2025.

Uthmeier’s catchy name was meant to grab attention, particularly from
President Donald Trump, who had recently [proposed
reopening](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/trump-says-
will-reopen-enlarged-rebuilt-alcatraz-prison-rcna204743) the notorious, [long-
shuttered Alcatraz federal
penitentiary](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/03/us/trump-alcatraz-
funding.html) in San Francisco Bay. During his first term, Trump had also
reportedly floated the idea of constructing [a moat filled with “snakes or
alligators”](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/01/us/politics/trump-border-
wars.html) to fortify his southern border wall. Keenly attuned to the power of
provocative branding, [Trump embraced Uthmeier’s
proposal](https://www.cbsnews.com/miami/news/floridas-attorney-general-faces-
new-attacks-over-alligator-alcatraz-and-hope-florida/).

Once given the green light, the administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis hastily
built a [makeshift detention center](https://www.cnn.com/2025/07/01/us/what-
is-alligator-alcatraz-florida) designed to hold several thousand migrants.
After touring the facility shortly before the first detainees arrived, [Trump
declared](https://apnews.com/article/florida-alligator-alcatraz-immigration-
detention-trump-desantis-cc060aa6528acbd91a87ec1922578146), “We’re surrounded
by miles of treacherous swampland, and the only way out is, really,
deportation.”

He added, “You have a lot of bodyguards and a lot of cops that are in the form
of alligators.”

Ahead of Trump’s visit, the Department of Homeland Security posted an [AI-
generated image](https://theconversation.com/alligator-alcatraz-showcases-
donald-trumps-penchant-for-visual-cruelty-260566) of menacing alligators
wearing Immigration and Customs Enforcement hats as they stood guard outside
the detention center. To cash in on the idea, the Florida Republican Party
also began peddling [Alligator Alcatraz–themed
merchandise](https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/5378520-florida-republican-
party-merchandise-migrant-facility/), like T-shirts, hats and beer koozies.

**The myth of crocodilians craving Black bodies**

Whether he realized it or not, Trump’s depiction of alligators as enforcers of
migrant detention echoed a much older tradition.

[My
research](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/G/bo268426675.html)
reveals that, as early as the 18th century, French explorers and naturalists
began claiming that alligators and crocodiles showed a marked preference for
attacking and consuming people of African descent. Plantation owners in the
South eagerly repeated these stories because they discouraged enslaved people
from escaping into marshes and swamps, where pursuing them proved difficult.

The idea gained much wider traction after the Civil War. As formerly enslaved
people secured freedom and basic civil rights, pursued educational and
economic opportunities, and gained political power, many white Americans
sought to [reassert white
supremacy](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/575769/stony-the-road-by-
henry-louis-gates-jr/). They restricted voting rights, imposed Jim Crow
segregation and inflicted racial violence.

They also employed [demeaning racial
stereotypes](https://www.upress.virginia.edu/title/1326/) designed to
humiliate African Americans while undermining their claims to freedom, dignity
and citizenship. My work shows how the growing association between alligators
and Black bodies was part of this larger campaign to reinforce notions of
Black inferiority.

Many postwar accounts of alligator attacks centered on a [dated racist
slur](https://jimcrowmuseum.ferris.edu/antiblack/picaninny/homepage.htm) that
portrayed Black children as [less than
human](https://nyupress.org/9780814787083/racial-innocence/). Typically
depicted with exaggerated features and ragged clothing – or no clothing at all
– these children were often shown being [chased by
alligators](https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/b1402b90-c539-012f-c772-58d385a7bc34?canvasIndex=0)
or other wild animals. Such images rested on the dehumanizing assumption that
Black children were incapable of experiencing pain or suffering in the same
way as their white counterparts.

**‘Alligator bait’ as a racial slur**

Soon, stories about hunters [using Black children as
bait](https://esnpc.blogspot.com/2020/04/live-human-alligator-bait-fact-
or.html) to lure alligators also began circulating. Some particularly
improbable accounts claimed that African American mothers [rented out their
babies](https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uc1.c3465645&seq=113&q1=alligator)
to hunters seeking to attract the reptiles.

These stories represented a grotesque inversion of the lived experience of
slavery. For enslaved women, the [forced separation from their
children](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/606278/all-that-she-
carried-by-tiya-miles/) was among the institution’s most devastating
cruelties. By suggesting that Black women would willingly place their own
children in mortal danger for profit, such narratives provided yet another
means of humiliating, degrading and dehumanizing African Americans.

By the late 19th century, these ideas had crystallized into the racial slur
“[alligator bait](https://www.icp.org/browse/archive/objects/alligator-bait).”
The phrase fused long-standing claims that alligators preferred Black flesh
with newer stories of Black children being used to attract the reptiles. It
soon became a fixture of American popular culture, appearing regularly in
[newspapers](https://www.newspapers.com/image/76574009/), [editorial
cartoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator_bait#/media/File:Haiti_revolution_United_States_alligator_bait_editorial_cartoon.jpg),
[postcards](https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/b09dee30-2729-0132-45d3-58d385a7bbd0),
[photographs](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/resource/stereo.1s11592/),
[songs](https://levysheetmusic.mse.jhu.edu/collection/105/128) and [motion
pictures](https://catalog.afi.com/Film/43108-ALLIGATOR-BAIT).

Such imagery remained widespread until the modern Civil Rights Movement
rendered it increasingly unacceptable.

**Perpetuating a racist tradition**

The architects of Alligator Alcatraz may not have consciously sought to invoke
the history of “alligator bait” stereotypes. Yet [historical
symbols](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/history-of-the-
swastika) often outlive the contexts in which they were created, and the
American alligator bears the imprint of a long racial history.

Alligator Alcatraz drew upon a symbol shaped by generations of racial
exclusion and dehumanization. In transforming migrant detention into political
theater, the [now-closed
facility](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/18/shuttered-alligator-
alcatraz-leaves-complicated-legacy-in-florida-01001031) revealed a troubling
disregard for symbolism and history. It also betrayed the cruelty and
indignity that [spectacle-based approaches to immigration
enforcement](https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/the-purpose-of-trumps-
cruel-deportation-theater.html) inflict on human beings.

The [tents may be gone](https://www.miamiherald.com/news/politics-
government/article316491685.html), but the racist historical echoes embedded
in the name “Alligator Alcatraz” remain.![The
Conversation](https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288043/count.gif?distributor=republish-
lightbox-basic)
